# Efficient Fable

Use Claude Fable as the orchestrator, architect, synthesizer, and final judge.
Use cheaper subagents for token-heavy research, coding, testing, and
summarization that do not require Fable's full judgment.

## Where Fable Shines

Reserve Fable for:

- Decomposing ambiguous work into clean parallel slices.
- Architecture, product, and safety tradeoffs.
- Reading conflicting subagent reports and deciding what matters.
- Integrating partial implementations into one coherent plan.
- Final review, risk assessment, and user-facing synthesis.

## Delegation Pattern

1. Name the expensive-token risk: large repo search, long logs, broad docs, or
   repetitive edits.
2. Split independent work into subagents before reading everything yourself.
3. Use cheaper models for research scans, inventory, search summaries, narrow
   bug hunts, browser/testing passes, test output reduction, and bounded code
   edits.
4. Ask subagents for concise evidence: files, line references, commands run,
   diffs, uncertainties, and stop conditions they hit.
5. Spend Fable tokens on the decision layer: compare results, resolve conflicts,
   choose the implementation path, and review the final patch.

Prefer parallel subagents when the slices do not depend on each other. Keep
blocking or highly coupled work local.

## Handoff Packets

Write delegated prompts as if the subagent has no useful chat context. Include
only the context it needs:

- The repo path and exact objective.
- The files, packages, or surfaces in scope and anything explicitly out of
  scope.
- The evidence format to return: files, line refs, commands, diffs, failures,
  screenshots, and uncertainty.
- The verification commands or browser flows to run, plus what success should
  look like when that is knowable.
- Stop conditions: if the code does not match the prompt, a command fails after
  a reasonable retry, or the task needs out-of-scope files, stop and report
  instead of improvising.

## Vetting Delegated Work

Treat subagent reports as leads, not facts. Before using a high-impact finding,
opening a PR, or telling the user the work is done, Fable should reopen the
important cited files, confirm the relevant line refs or failures, and review
the final diff against the task. Let lighter agents gather signal; keep
truth-judgment with Fable.

## Common Scenarios

Treat these as soft defaults, not rigid rules:

- Research: ask lighter agents to scan docs, prior art, APIs, and repo surfaces;
  Fable decides what evidence changes the plan.
- Coding: give cheaper agents bounded edits or candidate patches; Fable owns
  shared-file coordination, integration, and final review.
- Testing: have Fable suggest the validation direction and the scripts or
  browser checks that matter. Let lighter agents run targeted tests, browser
  flows, screenshots, and log reduction, then report exact commands, failures,
  likely causes, and whether failures look flaky, environmental, or real.
- Debugging: use cheaper agents to cluster logs, reproduce issues, and try
  small fixes; Fable decides which diagnosis is most trustworthy.

If a task is tiny or the validation itself needs delicate judgment, keep it
with Fable.

## Diagram

Use `assets/fable-orchestrator.excalidraw` when a visual explanation helps.

## Claims

For codebase-heavy work, it is reasonable to describe this as up to 3-5x more
cost-efficient and 2-4x faster when independent research, coding, or testing
slices can run in parallel. Treat those as workload-dependent estimates, not
guarantees.

Good launch copy:

> Make Claude Fable more efficient by using cheaper subagents for token-heavy
> research, coding, and testing, saving Fable for judgment, architecture,
> synthesis, and final review.

## claude.ai Pepo
Pepo answers questions about a specific brand's collected social content: the TikTok and Instagram videos and Reddit threads in this workspace, plus the creators, products and competitors named in them.

USE THESE TOOLS, not web search, whenever the user asks about:
- what is trending, breaking out, or gaining attention (find_trending)
- share of voice, or how the brand compares with competitors (share_of_voice)
- what a competitor has been doing or what drove a change (competitor_report)
- what people say about a product or SKU, complaints, purchase drivers (product_insights)
- which creators to work with, seed, or avoid (find_creators)
- how a campaign or launch performed (campaign_report)
- the underlying videos themselves, or exporting them (list_records, export_dataset, search_videos)
- which subreddits and Reddit threads discuss the category (search_videos with platforms set to reddit)
- what people actually SAY or SHOW in the videos — transcripts, visuals, audio (ask_corpus)

Web search cannot answer these: it cannot access this workspace's collected videos. A general answer about category trends is not the same as an answer about what this brand collected, and substituting one for the other is the main way to be wrong here.

Every response states what it will not stand behind — thin samples, uncomparable periods, unattributed corpora, missing paid/organic data. Repeat those caveats rather than summarising them away; they are the product, not boilerplate.
Views are observed content views, never ad impressions.

# merry

iPhone companion for AI coding agents — mirror notifications, control
workspaces, navigate surfaces, paste photos and files, and send voice commands
from your phone. Fronts [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) and
[herdr](https://herdr.dev), together or on their own.

## Architecture

```
[cmux Mac app]  ─┐
                 ├─ Unix socket ─  [cmux-bridge]  ─ WebSocket/LAN ─  [merry iOS app]
[herdr daemon]  ─┘
```

- **`bridge/`** — Go binary (`cmux-bridge`) that connects to the local cmux
  and/or herdr socket and exposes a WebSocket server on the LAN. See
  [Using herdr](#using-herdr-instead-of-cmux) for the backend options.
- **`ios/`** — SwiftUI iPhone app (landscape, iOS 17+)
- **`shared/`** — Protocol documentation

> The binary, config directory, bundle id, and `cmux-bridge://` pairing scheme
> keep their `cmux` names for compatibility with existing installs and pairings;
> only the product name changed.

## Prerequisites

- A supported runtime on the Mac:
  - [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) with socket control enabled
    (**Settings > Socket Control > Password mode**), and/or
  - [herdr](https://herdr.dev) running (`herdr`)
- Go 1.21+ (to build the bridge)
- Xcode 15+ (to build the iOS app)
- macOS 13+
- iOS 17+
- Mac and iPhone on the same local network

## Setup

### 1. Build the bridge

```bash
cd bridge
go build -o cmux-bridge ./cmd/cmux-bridge
sudo mv cmux-bridge /usr/local/bin/
```

Or use the install script (builds + sets up LaunchAgent for auto-start on login).
Run it **as your normal user, not with `sudo`** — it installs a per-user
LaunchAgent, and it will ask for sudo only if `/usr/local/bin` needs it:

```bash
./scripts/install-bridge.sh            # LAN only
./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale  # LAN + remote access (recommended)
```

The script hard-kills any previous bridge process and waits for the port to free
before starting the freshly-built binary, then verifies it's listening (and, with
`--tailscale`, that the tailnet listener came up). This avoids a stale daemon
silently keeping the old binary alive — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### 2. First-time pairing

This only needs to be done once. It connects to cmux's socket, generates a token, and shows a QR code.

```bash
cmux-bridge --pair
```

You'll be prompted for the cmux socket password (if password mode is enabled in cmux Settings > Socket Control). Then a QR code appears in the terminal — keep it visible for the next step.

### 3. Build and run the iOS app

Open `ios/cmux.xcodeproj` in Xcode, select your iPhone, and run.

On first launch, tap "Scan QR Code" and scan the QR from step 2.

### 4. Start the bridge

After pairing, start the bridge (it stays running and the iOS app auto-connects):

```bash
cmux-bridge
```

If you used `install-bridge.sh`, the LaunchAgent starts it automatically on login. Otherwise, run `cmux-bridge` manually or add it to your shell startup.

### Troubleshooting

- **iOS shows "reconnecting"** — make sure `cmux-bridge` is running and cmux is open
- **Bridge shows "cannot connect to cmux socket"** — make sure cmux is running with socket control enabled, then re-pair with `cmux-bridge --pair`
- **Need to re-pair** — run `cmux-bridge --pair` again and scan the new QR code from the iOS app (Settings > Pair new device)
- **Rebuilt the bridge but nothing changed / Tailscale never starts** — a stale
  daemon may still be holding the port. The bridge binds LAN **before** starting
  the Tailscale listener and treats a LAN bind failure as fatal, so a leftover
  process on `:47821` makes the new binary exit with
  `lan listen :47821: bind: address already in use` *before* Tailscale ever
  comes up. `launchctl unload`/`kickstart -k` do **not** kill a process that has
  reparented to launchd (PPID 1). Fix it by hard-killing every instance, then
  reinstalling:

  ```bash
  pkill -f /usr/local/bin/cmux-bridge
  lsof -nP -iTCP:47821 -sTCP:LISTEN     # should print nothing
  ./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale
  ```

  Confirm both listeners are up:

  ```bash
  grep -E "ws: listening|tailscale: listening" ~/Library/Logs/cmux-bridge.log | tail -2
  # ws: listening on :47821 (LAN)
  # tailscale: listening on cmux-bridge.<tailnet>.ts.net:47821
  ```

**Goal:** Working Go bridge that connects to the cmux socket, polls for notifications, and exposes a WebSocket server on the local network with QR-code pairing.

**Deliverables:**
- `cmux-bridge` binary (single static binary, no dependencies)
- LaunchAgent plist + install script

**Success criteria:**

- New cmux notifications appear on the WebSocket within 2 seconds

## P-002: iOS App Phase 1

**Goal:** SwiftUI iPhone app that pairs via QR, auto-discovers bridge on LAN, mirrors notifications, and can control workspaces/surfaces.

**Goal:** Add `notification.subscribe` to the cmux v2 socket API so the bridge can receive push events instead of polling.

**Deliverables:**

# herdr as a second backend for the companion app

Investigation date: 2026-08-24. herdr 0.8.2 (protocol 20) probed live on this Mac
via `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`; source read from github.com/herdrdev/herdr.

## Status (2026-08-24): Phases 0–2 implemented and verified live

- **Phase 0** — `bridge/internal/backend` (`Backend` interface, `Hub`,
  `Capabilities`); today's cmux code wrapped as `backend/cmux`; `ws` dispatches
  through the interface; `connected` payload carries `backend`,
  `backend_connected`, `capabilities`, `protocol_version: 2`; push events
  renamed `backend.connected/disconnected`. Config `backend` (auto/cmux/herdr),
  `herdr_socket_path`, `herdr_session`; flags `--backend`, `--config-dir`.
- **Phase 1** — `backend/herdr`: per-request socket client, lifecycle event
  subscription + snapshot-seeded pane cache, **one `pane.agent_status_changed`
  subscription per pane** (herdr scopes that event to a single pane_id, and does
  not emit `pane.updated` for status changes — found live), notifications
  synthesised from blocked/done transitions, `surface.updated` pushes, the full
  translation table below, viewport clamp for agent reads, transcript via the
  existing resolver. Unit tests against a fake herdr socket; verified
  end-to-end against the real herdr with a WebSocket client
  (workspaces/surfaces/layout/read/transcript/errors, and the
  working→blocked→done notification chain).
- **Phase 2** — iOS: `BackendCapabilities` + `backend` from `connected`,
  `surface.updated` handled, runtime `agent_status` drives the working
  indicator when the backend has it, `backend.*` and `cmux.*` pushes both
  accepted, unknown pushes ignored (previously mis-parsed as
  `notification.cleared`), status bar names the runtime, Settings shows the
  backend per bridge, pairing URL carries `backend=`.
- **Composite (2026-08-26)** — `backend/multi`: one bridge fronts cmux *and*
  herdr at once. Ids namespaced `cmux:<uuid>` / `herdr:w1:p1` in results,
  params and pushes; `workspace.list`/`notification.list` merged, titles
  suffixed ` · cmux`/` · herdr`; id-less commands follow the last
  `workspace.select`; `backend.disconnected` only when both are down. Config
  `backend: auto` = every runtime that answers, `all` = both regardless.
  Verified live against both runtimes (6 cmux + 3 herdr workspaces).
  Phone side: `RuntimeFilter` (All / cmux / herdr, persisted in UserDefaults)
  filters `visibleWorkspaces`; switcher in the sidebar menu and in Settings;
  workspace titles labelled ` · <runtime>` in All mode; a tapped alert from a
  hidden runtime switches the filter to it.
- **Not done (Phase 3)**: herdr tabs beyond the active one; ANSI terminal
  frames; neutral wire vocabulary; `surface.paste_image` for herdr (the
  feature lives on the unmerged `feat/paste-image` branch — same path-paste
  approach applies).

## TL;DR

- herdr is the same *shape* of thing as cmux for our purposes: a local daemon
  owning terminals, driven over a Unix socket with newline-delimited JSON, with a
  workspace → tab → pane tree, per-pane agent detection, and an event stream.
- It exposes **nothing over the network** (remote is SSH-only), so the bridge
  daemon keeps its job: sit on the Mac, talk to the local socket, expose the
  WebSocket to the phone over LAN/Tailscale.
- The companion has **no backend abstraction today**. `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go`
  `proxyCommand` forwards every phone command verbatim to `socket.Client`
  (cmux), and the iOS app's ~19 call sites speak cmux method names directly.
  Adding herdr means introducing that seam.
- Recommended path: a Go `Backend` interface + a `herdr` implementation that
  **translates the existing phone vocabulary** (`workspace.list`,
  `surface.read_text`, …) onto herdr's API. The phone changes are small
  (backend kind + capability flags in `connected`, hide browser affordances,
  optionally consume herdr's real agent status). Everything the app does today
  maps cleanly — see the table below. Two real gotchas are called out.

# merry

iPhone companion for AI coding agents — mirror notifications, control
workspaces, navigate surfaces, paste photos and files, and send voice commands
from your phone. Fronts [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) and
[herdr](https://herdr.dev), together or on their own.

## Architecture

```
[cmux Mac app]  ─┐
                 ├─ Unix socket ─  [cmux-bridge]  ─ WebSocket/LAN ─  [merry iOS app]
[herdr daemon]  ─┘
```

- **`bridge/`** — Go binary (`cmux-bridge`) that connects to the local cmux
  and/or herdr socket and exposes a WebSocket server on the LAN. See
  [Using herdr](#using-herdr-instead-of-cmux) for the backend options.
- **`ios/`** — SwiftUI iPhone app (landscape, iOS 17+)
- **`shared/`** — Protocol documentation

> The binary, config directory, bundle id, and `cmux-bridge://` pairing scheme
> keep their `cmux` names for compatibility with existing installs and pairings;
> only the product name changed.

## Prerequisites

- A supported runtime on the Mac:
  - [cmux](https://github.com/manaflow-ai/cmux) with socket control enabled
    (**Settings > Socket Control > Password mode**), and/or
  - [herdr](https://herdr.dev) running (`herdr`)
- Go 1.21+ (to build the bridge)
- Xcode 15+ (to build the iOS app)
- macOS 13+
- iOS 17+
- Mac and iPhone on the same local network

## Setup

### 1. Build the bridge

```bash
cd bridge
go build -o cmux-bridge ./cmd/cmux-bridge
sudo mv cmux-bridge /usr/local/bin/
```

Or use the install script (builds + sets up LaunchAgent for auto-start on login).
Run it **as your normal user, not with `sudo`** — it installs a per-user
LaunchAgent, and it will ask for sudo only if `/usr/local/bin` needs it:

```bash
./scripts/install-bridge.sh            # LAN only
./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale  # LAN + remote access (recommended)
```

The script hard-kills any previous bridge process and waits for the port to free
before starting the freshly-built binary, then verifies it's listening (and, with
`--tailscale`, that the tailnet listener came up). This avoids a stale daemon
silently keeping the old binary alive — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### 2. First-time pairing

This only needs to be done once. It connects to cmux's socket, generates a token, and shows a QR code.

```bash
cmux-bridge --pair
```

You'll be prompted for the cmux socket password (if password mode is enabled in cmux Settings > Socket Control). Then a QR code appears in the terminal — keep it visible for the next step.

### 3. Build and run the iOS app

Open `ios/cmux.xcodeproj` in Xcode, select your iPhone, and run.

On first launch, tap "Scan QR Code" and scan the QR from step 2.

### 4. Start the bridge

After pairing, start the bridge (it stays running and the iOS app auto-connects):

```bash
cmux-bridge
```

If you used `install-bridge.sh`, the LaunchAgent starts it automatically on login. Otherwise, run `cmux-bridge` manually or add it to your shell startup.

### Troubleshooting

- **iOS shows "reconnecting"** — make sure `cmux-bridge` is running and cmux is open
- **Bridge shows "cannot connect to cmux socket"** — make sure cmux is running with socket control enabled, then re-pair with `cmux-bridge --pair`
- **Need to re-pair** — run `cmux-bridge --pair` again and scan the new QR code from the iOS app (Settings > Pair new device)
- **Rebuilt the bridge but nothing changed / Tailscale never starts** — a stale
  daemon may still be holding the port. The bridge binds LAN **before** starting
  the Tailscale listener and treats a LAN bind failure as fatal, so a leftover
  process on `:47821` makes the new binary exit with
  `lan listen :47821: bind: address already in use` *before* Tailscale ever
  comes up. `launchctl unload`/`kickstart -k` do **not** kill a process that has
  reparented to launchd (PPID 1). Fix it by hard-killing every instance, then
  reinstalling:

  ```bash
  pkill -f /usr/local/bin/cmux-bridge
  lsof -nP -iTCP:47821 -sTCP:LISTEN     # should print nothing
  ./scripts/install-bridge.sh --tailscale
  ```

  Confirm both listeners are up:

  ```bash
  grep -E "ws: listening|tailscale: listening" ~/Library/Logs/cmux-bridge.log | tail -2
  # ws: listening on :47821 (LAN)
  # tailscale: listening on cmux-bridge.<tailnet>.ts.net:47821
  ```

# herdr as a second backend for the companion app

Investigation date: 2026-08-24. herdr 0.8.2 (protocol 20) probed live on this Mac
via `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`; source read from github.com/herdrdev/herdr.

## Status (2026-08-24): Phases 0–2 implemented and verified live

- **Phase 0** — `bridge/internal/backend` (`Backend` interface, `Hub`,
  `Capabilities`); today's cmux code wrapped as `backend/cmux`; `ws` dispatches
  through the interface; `connected` payload carries `backend`,
  `backend_connected`, `capabilities`, `protocol_version: 2`; push events
  renamed `backend.connected/disconnected`. Config `backend` (auto/cmux/herdr),
  `herdr_socket_path`, `herdr_session`; flags `--backend`, `--config-dir`.
- **Phase 1** — `backend/herdr`: per-request socket client, lifecycle event
  subscription + snapshot-seeded pane cache, **one `pane.agent_status_changed`
  subscription per pane** (herdr scopes that event to a single pane_id, and does
  not emit `pane.updated` for status changes — found live), notifications
  synthesised from blocked/done transitions, `surface.updated` pushes, the full
  translation table below, viewport clamp for agent reads, transcript via the
  existing resolver. Unit tests against a fake herdr socket; verified
  end-to-end against the real herdr with a WebSocket client
  (workspaces/surfaces/layout/read/transcript/errors, and the
  working→blocked→done notification chain).
- **Phase 2** — iOS: `BackendCapabilities` + `backend` from `connected`,
  `surface.updated` handled, runtime `agent_status` drives the working
  indicator when the backend has it, `backend.*` and `cmux.*` pushes both
  accepted, unknown pushes ignored (previously mis-parsed as
  `notification.cleared`), status bar names the runtime, Settings shows the
  backend per bridge, pairing URL carries `backend=`.
- **Composite (2026-08-26)** — `backend/multi`: one bridge fronts cmux *and*
  herdr at once. Ids namespaced `cmux:<uuid>` / `herdr:w1:p1` in results,
  params and pushes; `workspace.list`/`notification.list` merged, titles
  suffixed ` · cmux`/` · herdr`; id-less commands follow the last
  `workspace.select`; `backend.disconnected` only when both are down. Config
  `backend: auto` = every runtime that answers, `all` = both regardless.
  Verified live against both runtimes (6 cmux + 3 herdr workspaces).
  Phone side: `RuntimeFilter` (All / cmux / herdr, persisted in UserDefaults)
  filters `visibleWorkspaces`; switcher in the sidebar menu and in Settings;
  workspace titles labelled ` · <runtime>` in All mode; a tapped alert from a
  hidden runtime switches the filter to it.
- **Not done (Phase 3)**: herdr tabs beyond the active one; ANSI terminal
  frames; neutral wire vocabulary; `surface.paste_image` for herdr (the
  feature lives on the unmerged `feat/paste-image` branch — same path-paste
  approach applies).

## TL;DR

- herdr is the same *shape* of thing as cmux for our purposes: a local daemon
  owning terminals, driven over a Unix socket with newline-delimited JSON, with a
  workspace → tab → pane tree, per-pane agent detection, and an event stream.
- It exposes **nothing over the network** (remote is SSH-only), so the bridge
  daemon keeps its job: sit on the Mac, talk to the local socket, expose the
  WebSocket to the phone over LAN/Tailscale.
- The companion has **no backend abstraction today**. `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go`
  `proxyCommand` forwards every phone command verbatim to `socket.Client`
  (cmux), and the iOS app's ~19 call sites speak cmux method names directly.
  Adding herdr means introducing that seam.
- Recommended path: a Go `Backend` interface + a `herdr` implementation that
  **translates the existing phone vocabulary** (`workspace.list`,
  `surface.read_text`, …) onto herdr's API. The phone changes are small
  (backend kind + capability flags in `connected`, hide browser affordances,
  optionally consume herdr's real agent status). Everything the app does today
  maps cleanly — see the table below. Two real gotchas are called out.

## herdr facts that matter

| Topic | Fact | Verified how |
|---|---|---|
| Socket | `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock` (named sessions: `~/.config/herdr/sessions/<name>/herdr.sock`); env override `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`; mode 0600, no auth | `src/server/socket_paths.rs`, `src/session.rs`, live |
| Wire | NDJSON. Req `{"id","method","params"}` → `{"id","result":{"type":…}}` or `{"id","error":{"code","message"}}`. Server closes after one-shot responses → **one connection per request**, like herdr's own `ApiClient`. Subscriptions keep the connection open. | `src/api/client.rs`, live |
| Handshake | `ping` → `{"type":"pong","version":"0.8.2","protocol":20,"capabilities":{…}}` | live |
| Model | workspace `w1` → tab `w1:t1` → pane `w1:p1` (one terminal per pane). `terminal_id` is stable across pane moves; `pane_id` changes on cross-workspace `pane.move`. | `src/api/schema/*.rs`, live |
| Bootstrap | `session.snapshot` → workspaces, tabs, panes, per-tab layouts (pane rects in cells + tab `area`), agents, focused ids | live |
| Push | `events.subscribe` with a list of subscriptions. Global ones (`pane.updated`, `pane.created/closed/focused`, `workspace.*`, `tab.*`, `layout.updated`) need no filter; `pane.agent_status_changed` and `pane.scroll_changed` require a `pane_id`. First line is `{"type":"subscription_started"}`, then `{"event":"pane_updated","data":{…PaneInfo}}`. No replay. | `src/api/schema/events.rs`, live |
| **No output push** | `pane.output_changed` exists as an `EventKind` but is not subscribable and `events.wait` rejects it ("currently supports pane agent status matches"). `PaneInfo.revision` is a *state* revision, not an output counter (stayed 0 after 500 lines). ⇒ live text stays **poll-based**, as with cmux. | live |
| Read | `pane.read {pane_id, source, lines?, format?, strip_ansi?}` → `result.read.text`, `truncated`. Sources on the wire: `visible`, `recent`, `recent_unwrapped` (underscore! CLI spells it with a dash), `detection`. `recent` + `lines:N` includes host scrollback (400/500 lines came back; `scroll.max_offset_from_bottom` = 460). Default 80 rows. | live |
| **Alt-screen agents** | For an *idle* recognized agent (Claude Code, opencode…) a `recent` read with `lines` > viewport makes herdr **drive the agent's mouse-scroll to page history, then scroll back to bottom** — i.e. it visibly moves the user's live pane. While *working* it just returns the visible screen (got 40 lines for `lines:400`). ⇒ for agent panes the bridge must clamp `lines` to `scroll.viewport_rows` or use `source:"visible"`, and get history from the transcript (which the phone already prefers for Claude). | `docs/…/agent-automation.mdx`, live |
| Input | `pane.send_text {text}` literal; `pane.send_keys {keys:[…]}`; `pane.send_input {text, keys}`. Key names: `enter`/`return`, `esc`/`escape`, `tab`, `shift+tab`, `backspace`, `up/down/left/right`, `ctrl+x`, `alt+x`, `f1`, `space`, `minus`… (`src/config/keybinds.rs` `parse_key_combo`). `agent.prompt {target,text}` = text + Enter, bracketed-paste aware, returns `agent_blocked` instead of typing into an approval dialog. | schema, live |
| Agent status | Per pane/tab/workspace: `idle` / `working` / `blocked` / `done` / `unknown`. From hooks when an integration is installed, else from screen manifests. Rolls up to workspace. `done` = finished and not yet looked at. | `docs/concepts.mdx`, live |
| Agent kind | `PaneInfo.agent` (`"claude"`, `"codex"`, `"opencode"`, … 20+ kinds) | live |
| Session binding | `herdr integration install claude` installs `~/.claude/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh` (+ `settings.json` hooks). It sends `pane.report_agent_session {agent_session_id, agent_session_path}` — but herdr **keeps only the id** for claude (`src/agent_resume.rs` `session_ref_from_report` drops the path). Exposed as `pane.agent_session: {source:"herdr:claude", agent:"claude", kind:"id", value:"<uuid>"}` on `pane.get/list`, `agent.get/list`. Not installed on this Mac yet (`herdr integration status`). | source, live |
| Notifications | None as a list. Derive from `pane.updated` / `pane.agent_status_changed` transitions to `blocked` / `done`. `notification.show` exists but is herdr→user toast, the wrong direction. | schema |
| Browser surfaces | None; terminal-only. | — |
| Image paste | herdr's own remote-attach does what our `feat/paste-image` does: write the image to a temp file on the host and paste the *path*. Same plan: bridge writes the file, `pane.send_text` the path. | `docs/persistence-remote.mdx` |
| Terminal frames (future) | `herdr terminal session observe w1:p1 --cols --rows` streams NDJSON `terminal.frame` records (base64 ANSI) "for third-party bridges that only need rendered terminal bytes"; `control` adds input/resize. This is the private client-socket protocol (`herdr-client.sock`, `src/protocol/wire.rs`), reachable via the CLI as a subprocess. It's the path to a real terminal emulator view on the phone later. | docs |
| Layout ops | `pane.split {target_pane_id, direction: right\|down, focus}`, `pane.close`, `pane.focus`, `workspace.focus/create/close`, `tab.create`. | schema |

## Companion facts that matter (from the code map)

- Bridge: `bridge/cmd/cmux-bridge/main.go` (`runDaemon` :287), `bridge/internal/socket/client.go` (concrete cmux client: socket detection, `auth.login`, `{ok,result,error}` envelope), `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go` (`proxyCommand` :219, `claude.transcript` special-case :119), `bridge/internal/poller/poller.go` (polls `notification.list` every 1s, `Broadcast` is the only fan-out seam), `bridge/internal/claude/` (transcript resolver; strategies `hook_store_surface`, `hook_store_session`, `projects_glob`, `cwd_latest`).
- Phone: `ios/cmux/App/AppState.swift` — models `Workspace {id,title}`, `Surface {id,title,type,workspace_id,is_focused,resume_binding.kind}`, `Pane {id,pixel_frame,container_frame,surface_ids,focused_surface_id,is_focused}`, `BridgeNotification {id,title,subtitle,body,workspace_id,surface_id}`. Working indicator is a diff-of-successive-reads heuristic (`setWorking`). Keys sent: `ctrl+c/d/l/z`, `enter`, `return`, `tab`, `esc`, `escape`, `up/down/left/right`, `space`, `cmd+shift+enter`.
- Identity: `PairingCredentials {host,port,token,tailscaleHost}` — no backend kind. `connected` push carries `cmux_connected`, no capabilities.
- Precedent for "two implementations behind one wire method": branch `worktree-opencode-sessions`, `bridge/internal/ws/transcript.go` (`agentTranscripts` if-chain).

## Plan

### Phase 0 — the seam (bridge only, no behavior change)

1. `bridge/internal/backend/backend.go`:
   ```go
   type Backend interface {
       Connect(ctx) error; Close() error
       Ping() error
       Handle(method string, params map[string]any) (json.RawMessage, *RPCError)  // phone vocabulary in, phone vocabulary out
       Events() <-chan Event   // notification.created, surface.updated, backend.connected/disconnected
       Info() Info             // Kind ("cmux"|"herdr"), Version, Capabilities{Browser, Tabs, AgentStatus, Notifications}
   }
   ```
2. Move today's behavior into `backend/cmux` (wraps `socket.Client` + `poller.Poller` unchanged).
3. `runDaemon` picks the backend from config `backend: "cmux"|"herdr"|"auto"` (auto: herdr if `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock` connects, else cmux). New keys: `herdr_socket_path`, `herdr_session`.
4. `connected` payload gains `backend`, `backend_connected` (keep `cmux_connected` as an alias for one release), `capabilities`.

### Phase 1 — `backend/herdr`

Client: per-request Unix connection (`net.Dial("unix")`, write line, read line), plus one long-lived subscriber connection running `events.subscribe` on `pane.updated`, `pane.created`, `pane.closed`, `pane.focused`, `workspace.*`, `tab.*`, `layout.updated`; reconnect with backoff; `ping` health like today's 5s loop.

Translation table (phone method → herdr):

| Phone (unchanged) | herdr | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `system.ping` | `ping` | |
| `workspace.list` | `workspace.list` | `{id: workspace_id, title: label}` |
| `workspace.current` | snapshot `focused_workspace_id` | |
| `workspace.select` | `workspace.focus` | |
| `workspace.create {name}` | `workspace.create {label, cwd:$HOME}` | |
| `workspace.close` | `workspace.close` | |
| `surface.list {workspace_id}` | `pane.list {workspace_id}` | surface = pane: `{id: pane_id, title: terminal_title_stripped ?? label ?? basename(foreground_cwd), type:"terminal", workspace_id, is_focused: focused, resume_binding: {kind: agent, checkpoint_id: agent_session.value}}` + new `agent_status` |
| `surface.focus` / `surface.close` | `pane.focus` / `pane.close` | |
| `surface.split {direction}` | `pane.split {target_pane_id, direction}` | left/up → right/down (herdr only splits right/down) |
| `surface.create {type:"terminal"}` | `tab.create` in the surface's workspace | browser → error `unsupported` |
| `surface.read_text {surface_id, lines}` | `pane.read {source:"recent", lines}` | **If `pane.agent != nil`: `lines = min(lines, scroll.viewport_rows)`** (gotcha above). Return `{text}`. |
| `surface.send_text {text}` | `pane.send_text` | |
| `surface.send_key {key}` | `pane.send_keys {keys:[map(key)]}` | `escape→esc`, `return→enter`, `cmd+shift+enter→enter`; else pass through |
| `surface.paste_image` | write temp file, `pane.send_text path` | reuse `internal/imagepaste` from `feat/paste-image` |
| `pane.list {workspace_id}` | snapshot/`pane.layout` for the workspace's **active tab** | `{id: pane_id, pixel_frame: rect, container_frame: {width,height} of tab area, surface_ids:[pane_id], focused_surface_id: pane_id, is_focused}`. Phone's `normalizedFrame` handles cell units. Non-active tabs: v2 (expose as extra "panes" or a tab strip). |
| `pane.focus` | `pane.focus` | |
| `notification.list` / `notification.clear` | in-memory list synthesized from event stream | see below |
| `claude.transcript` (`agent.transcript`) | `pane.get` → `agent_session.value` → `claude.Resolver` by session id (`projects_glob` under `~/.claude/projects/*/<id>.jsonl`) | Add a resolver entry point that takes a session id from the backend instead of the cmux hook store. Requires `herdr integration install claude` on the Mac; bridge should detect the missing `agent_session` and return `supported:false, reason:"install herdr claude integration"`. |

Notifications: keep a per-pane last `agent_status`; on `pane.updated` where status becomes `blocked` emit `notification.created {id: "<pane_id>:<state_change_seq>", title: terminal_title_stripped ?? agent, subtitle: workspace label, body: "needs your input", workspace_id, surface_id}`; on `done` emit "finished". `notification.clear` empties the list. This is strictly better than cmux's polled list — real push, sub-second.

### Phase 2 — phone

1. `ConnectedPayload`: `backend`, `capabilities`; `PairingCredentials`/`SavedBridge` show the kind in Settings; pairing URL keeps `cmux-bridge://` (rename later) but gains `kind=`.
2. Hide browser affordances (`Surface.isBrowser`, `browser.url.get`) when `capabilities.browser == false`.
3. Prefer `surface.agent_status` from herdr over the read-diff `setWorking` heuristic when present; show `blocked` as the attention state (it's what the "stuck one" badge in herdr's sidebar is).
4. `isClaudeAgent` already keys off `resume_binding.kind`, so the transcript button lights up unchanged once the bridge fills it in.

### Phase 3 — later

<result># Research Report: mosh, Moshi, herdr, and alternatives for responsive terminal streaming

## 1. mosh (mobile shell)

- **What it is / transport**: Mosh runs `mosh-server` on the remote host and `mosh-client` locally; SSH is used only to bootstrap (authenticate and launch the server, which picks a UDP port in range 60000–61000), after which all traffic is UDP encrypted/authenticated with AES-128-OCB3 via the custom **State Synchronization Protocol (SSP)**. [mosh.org](https://mosh.org/), [Mosh paper (USENIX ATC'12)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc12/technical-sessions/presentation/winstein), [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf)
- **How state sync works — CONFIRMED**: The server runs a real terminal emulator; both server and client hold a "screen state" object (not a byte stream). SSP's job is to fast-forward the client's screen-state object to match the server's, skipping intermediate frames if needed, and controls its own "frame rate" so it never floods the network — it does not have to forward every byte the shell produces. [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf), [GitHub issue #1087 on SSP](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/1087)
- **Roaming/benefits**: client sends increasing sequence numbers plus heartbeats every ≤3s; the server retargets outgoing packets to whatever source IP sent the latest authenticated packet, giving seamless roaming across networks/sleep. Predictive local echo overlays keystrokes client-side before server ack. [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf)
- **Scrollback — CONFIRMED NO SUPPORT, long-standing**: GitHub **issue #2** ("Scrollback and alternate screen"), open since Oct 2011, is the canonical tracking issue; the FAQ explicitly points to it. Because mosh only ever syncs the *current* screen-state object, there is no host-side byte history to scroll into — this is architectural, not a missing feature. [Issue #2](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/2), [Issue #865 "Scrollback still not working in 1.3"](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/865), [Moshi's own explainer](https://getmoshi.app/articles/fix-mosh-scrollback)
- **Mosh 1.4 (Oct 2022) changes**: added **24-bit/true color** support, OSC 52 clipboard integration, `--predict-overwrite` prediction mode, syslog logging — but did **not** add scrollback. Mouse reporting support predates 1.4 (added in 1.2.5, 2015). Unicode/UTF-8 support has been present from early on; no major Unicode change noted in 1.4. [mosh-1.4.0-released.html](https://mosh.org/mosh-1.4.0-released.html), [ChangeLog](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/blob/master/ChangeLog), [Issue #649 24-bit color](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/649)
- **Limitation vs. tmux control mode**: mosh does not support `tmux -CC` control mode because that expects a reliable stream channel; mosh's UDP/lossy-tolerant design is fundamentally incompatible with it. [HN discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25740217)

## 2. Client-side mosh implementations for iOS/Swift and Go

- **Blink Shell**: open source (github.com/blinksh/blink), licensed **GPLv3 with OpenSSL/iOS exceptions** (inherited from mosh's own license). Wraps a C++ port called **libmoshios** (plus libssh2, OpenSSL, protobuf, ios_system) rather than a pure-Swift reimplementation. [blinksh/blink](https://github.com/blinksh/blink), [blink.sh](https://blink.sh/), [Mosh license note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosh_(software))
- **Licensing implication for merry**: mosh itself is **GPLv3**. Any embedded mosh client (Blink's libmoshios or the mosh C++ code directly) would pull GPLv3 obligations into the app unless isolated as a separate process/IPC boundary — a real constraint for a proprietary iOS app.
- **Go implementations**: no native pure-Go mosh; found **`go-mosh`** (github.com/thyth/go-mosh) — a SWIG wrapper exposing mosh's C++ prediction/emulation engine to Go, itself GPLv3 since it links mosh code. Another Go wrapper (`github.com/artyom/mosh`) is just a CLI convenience wrapper around the system `mosh` binary, not a protocol reimplementation. No credible "gomosh" pure-protocol reimplementation was found — UNVERIFIED that one exists. [go-mosh](https://github.com/thyth/go-mosh), [artyom/mosh](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/artyom/mosh)
- **Termius**: claims mosh support in its product but no open-source implementation details found; UNVERIFIED internals.
- **Embedding difficulty**: given GPLv3 + the need for a full server-side terminal-emulation engine (not just protocol code) plus SSP, embedding mosh client logic in a SwiftUI app is a substantial lift — realistically means vendoring Blink's libmoshios (C++) via a bridging layer, and accepting GPLv3 obligations, or writing your own SSP+terminal-emulation client from scratch (mosh has no thin client library).

## 3. The Moshi app

- **App**: "Moshi: herdr/tmux on SSH/MOSH", App Store id 6757859949, publisher **Moshi Tech Ltd**; also on Google Play (`app.getmoshi.android`). Docs/marketing site: getmoshi.app. [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moshi-herdr-tmux-on-ssh-mosh/id6757859949), [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.getmoshi.android), [getmoshi.app](https://getmoshi.app/)
- **What it does**: SSH/Mosh terminal client tuned for checking on AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Aider) from a phone; a "Session Switcher" jumps between tmux windows or Herdr tabs; on-device Whisper voice-to-terminal; SSH keys in iOS Keychain with biometrics. [App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moshi-herdr-tmux-on-ssh-mosh/id6757859949)
- **Scrollback mechanism — directly answers the pain point**: Moshi does **not** solve mosh's lack of scrollback via any clever protocol trick. It (a) keeps a small **in-app scrollback buffer** (configurable line limit, but only content seen since session start/reconnect — not host history), and (b) for real host-side history, relies on the **underlying multiplexer** (tmux copy-mode, or Herdr's own scrollback) and tunes touch gestures around whichever is detected: drag-to-scroll on the raw terminal forwards mouse-wheel events into tmux, and Moshi explicitly detects tmux copy mode to adapt touch scrolling. Its own docs state plainly: *"The mosh protocol does not transmit scrollback... only the current visible screen is restored"* on reconnect. [Scrolling docs](https://getmoshi.app/docs/scrolling), [Fix Mosh Scrollback article](https://getmoshi.app/articles/fix-mosh-scrollback)
- **tmux vs Herdr framing**: Moshi's own guide says tmux "keeps processes alive and tells you nothing about them," while Herdr "tracks which agent panes are blocked, working, or done"; Herdr offers "standard scrollback" that's "clickable by design," plus purpose-built APIs (wait-on-status, read-pane-output) versus tmux's send-keys scripting. [tmux-or-herdr guide](https://getmoshi.app/guides/tmux-or-herdr)
- **Terminal emulator / rendering tech**: **not disclosed** in any fetched docs page — UNVERIFIED which VT/ANSI rendering library Moshi uses.
- **Who makes it**: Publisher is "Moshi Tech Ltd." No page found stating a relationship to the herdr authors (herdrdev/herdr on GitHub); Moshi's own comparison guide treats Herdr as a third-party integration, not its own product — **appears to be an independent company**, UNVERIFIED beyond that (no explicit "we are/aren't affiliated" statement found).

## 4. herdr's remote/terminal-streaming APIs (github.com/herdrdev/herdr, herdr.dev)

- **CLI streaming commands** (confirmed via herdr.dev/docs/cli-reference): 
  - `herdr terminal session observe <target> [--cols N] [--rows N]` — read-only NDJSON stream of `terminal.frame` records (base64-encoded ANSI bytes), ending in `terminal.closed`; multiple observers allowed concurrently.
  - `herdr terminal session control <target> [--takeover] [--cols N] [--rows N]` — writable stream; accepts NDJSON commands `terminal.input`, `terminal.resize`, `terminal.scroll`, `terminal.release`; single controller unless `--takeover`.
  [CLI reference](https://herdr.dev/docs/cli-reference/)
- **Socket API** (herdr.dev/docs/socket-api): NDJSON over local Unix sockets, default `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock` (named sessions under `~/.config/herdr/sessions/<name>/herdr.sock`). `PaneInfo` carries scroll metrics: `{"offset_from_bottom": 12, "max_offset_from_bottom": 240, "viewport_rows": 30}`, with `offset_from_bottom == 0` meaning at-bottom. Event subscription `pane.scroll_changed` pushes these metrics on change (plus `pane.created/updated/closed/focused/moved/exited/agent_detected/output_matched/agent_status_changed`). [Socket API docs](https://herdr.dev/docs/socket-api/)
- **Remote/mobile**: docs mention `herdr --remote workbox` (SSH-based attach to a remote herdr instance using local keybindings) and a `--handoff` flag for live session transfer to an updated server — but no herdr-native mobile/WebSocket client was found; no `herdr-client.sock` or `persistence-remote` terminology was found in fetched docs (UNVERIFIED / may not exist as named). No `pane.scroll` command name was found distinct from `terminal.scroll`; treat `pane.scroll` as UNVERIFIED naming vs. confirmed `terminal.scroll`.

## 5. Prior art: server-side state + diff sync over a plain socket

- **tmux control mode (`tmux -CC`)**: server-authoritative pane state pushed over a control protocol to a client (used by iTerm2); relevant precedent for "diff-sync over a normal reliable socket," but requires a reliable stream (works over SSH/WS, not suited to lossy mobile links the way mosh is). [HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25740217)
- **Eternal Terminal (ET)**: TCP-based persistent-session tool; includes a "headless terminal multiplexer" (HTM) that tracks tab/pane state so a client reattaching gets restored state — closer analog to what merry wants (state resync over TCP/WS) but ET itself doesn't do frame-diffing the way mosh does. [eternalterminal.dev](https://eternalterminal.dev/)
- **xterm.js `addon-serialize`**: serializes an xterm.js buffer (screen + alt-screen + cursor) to a string/HTML blob for restore; directly relevant as a pattern for "reconstruct full terminal state from a snapshot," though it's a JS/web library, marked experimental. [addon-serialize](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/tree/master/addons/addon-serialize)
- **ttyd, wezterm mux, ghostty**: no strong documentary evidence surfaced in this pass connecting them to a diff-sync architecture comparable to mosh/SSP — UNVERIFIED, would need dedicated follow-up if wanted.

## 6. iOS terminal emulator libraries for SwiftUI

- **SwiftTerm** (migueldeicaza/SwiftTerm): MIT-licensed, mature (~7 years, 1300+ commits, 32 releases), includes a UI-agnostic VT100/xterm engine plus iOS (UIKit) and macOS (AppKit) front-ends usable from SwiftUI via wrapping. Used by commercial SSH apps: Secure Shellfish, La Terminal, CodeEdit. <result># Research Report: mosh, Moshi, herdr, and alternatives for responsive terminal streaming

## 1. mosh (mobile shell)

- **What it is / transport**: Mosh runs `mosh-server` on the remote host and `mosh-client` locally; SSH is used only to bootstrap (authenticate and launch the server, which picks a UDP port in range 60000–61000), after which all traffic is UDP encrypted/authenticated with AES-128-OCB3 via the custom **State Synchronization Protocol (SSP)**. [mosh.org](https://mosh.org/), [Mosh paper (USENIX ATC'12)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc12/technical-sessions/presentation/winstein), [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf)
- **How state sync works — CONFIRMED**: The server runs a real terminal emulator; both server and client hold a "screen state" object (not a byte stream). SSP's job is to fast-forward the client's screen-state object to match the server's, skipping intermediate frames if needed, and controls its own "frame rate" so it never floods the network — it does not have to forward every byte the shell produces. [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf), [GitHub issue #1087 on SSP](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/1087)
- **Roaming/benefits**: client sends increasing sequence numbers plus heartbeats every ≤3s; the server retargets outgoing packets to whatever source IP sent the latest authenticated packet, giving seamless roaming across networks/sleep. Predictive local echo overlays keystrokes client-side before server ack. [mosh-paper.pdf](https://mosh.org/mosh-paper.pdf)
- **Scrollback — CONFIRMED NO SUPPORT, long-standing**: GitHub **issue #2** ("Scrollback and alternate screen"), open since Oct 2011, is the canonical tracking issue; the FAQ explicitly points to it. Because mosh only ever syncs the *current* screen-state object, there is no host-side byte history to scroll into — this is architectural, not a missing feature. [Issue #2](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/2), [Issue #865 "Scrollback still not working in 1.3"](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/865), [Moshi's own explainer](https://getmoshi.app/articles/fix-mosh-scrollback)
- **Mosh 1.4 (Oct 2022) changes**: added **24-bit/true color** support, OSC 52 clipboard integration, `--predict-overwrite` prediction mode, syslog logging — but did **not** add scrollback. Mouse reporting support predates 1.4 (added in 1.2.5, 2015). Unicode/UTF-8 support has been present from early on; no major Unicode change noted in 1.4. [mosh-1.4.0-released.html](https://mosh.org/mosh-1.4.0-released.html), [ChangeLog](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/blob/master/ChangeLog), [Issue #649 24-bit color](https://github.com/mobile-shell/mosh/issues/649)
- **Limitation vs. tmux control mode**: mosh does not support `tmux -CC` control mode because that expects a reliable stream channel; mosh's UDP/lossy-tolerant design is fundamentally incompatible with it. [HN discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25740217)

## 2. Client-side mosh implementations for iOS/Swift and Go

- **Blink Shell**: open source (github.com/blinksh/blink), licensed **GPLv3 with OpenSSL/iOS exceptions** (inherited from mosh's own license). Wraps a C++ port called **libmoshios** (plus libssh2, OpenSSL, protobuf, ios_system) rather than a pure-Swift reimplementation. [blinksh/blink](https://github.com/blinksh/blink), [blink.sh](https://blink.sh/), [Mosh license note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosh_(software))
- **Licensing implication for merry**: mosh itself is **GPLv3**. Any embedded mosh client (Blink's libmoshios or the mosh C++ code directly) would pull GPLv3 obligations into the app unless isolated as a separate process/IPC boundary — a real constraint for a proprietary iOS app.
- **Go implementations**: no native pure-Go mosh; found **`go-mosh`** (github.com/thyth/go-mosh) — a SWIG wrapper exposing mosh's C++ prediction/emulation engine to Go, itself GPLv3 since it links mosh code. Another Go wrapper (`github.com/artyom/mosh`) is just a CLI convenience wrapper around the system `mosh` binary, not a protocol reimplementation. No credible "gomosh" pure-protocol reimplementation was found — UNVERIFIED that one exists. [go-mosh](https://github.com/thyth/go-mosh), [artyom/mosh](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/artyom/mosh)
- **Termius**: claims mosh support in its product but no open-source implementation details found; UNVERIFIED internals.
- **Embedding difficulty**: given GPLv3 + the need for a full server-side terminal-emulation engine (not just protocol code) plus SSP, embedding mosh client logic in a SwiftUI app is a substantial lift — realistically means vendoring Blink's libmoshios (C++) via a bridging layer, and accepting GPLv3 obligations, or writing your own SSP+terminal-emulation client from scratch (mosh has no thin client library).

## 3. The Moshi app

- **App**: "Moshi: herdr/tmux on SSH/MOSH", App Store id 6757859949, publisher **Moshi Tech Ltd**; also on Google Play (`app.getmoshi.android`). Docs/marketing site: getmoshi.app. [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moshi-herdr-tmux-on-ssh-mosh/id6757859949), [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.getmoshi.android), [getmoshi.app](https://getmoshi.app/)
- **What it does**: SSH/Mosh terminal client tuned for checking on AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Aider) from a phone; a "Session Switcher" jumps between tmux windows or Herdr tabs; on-device Whisper voice-to-terminal; SSH keys in iOS Keychain with biometrics. [App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moshi-herdr-tmux-on-ssh-mosh/id6757859949)
- **Scrollback mechanism — directly answers the pain point**: Moshi does **not** solve mosh's lack of scrollback via any clever protocol trick. It (a) keeps a small **in-app scrollback buffer** (configurable line limit, but only content seen since session start/reconnect — not host history), and (b) for real host-side history, relies on the **underlying multiplexer** (tmux copy-mode, or Herdr's own scrollback) and tunes touch gestures around whichever is detected: drag-to-scroll on the raw terminal forwards mouse-wheel events into tmux, and Moshi explicitly detects tmux copy mode to adapt touch scrolling. Its own docs state plainly: *"The mosh protocol does not transmit scrollback... only the current visible screen is restored"* on reconnect. [Scrolling docs](https://getmoshi.app/docs/scrolling), [Fix Mosh Scrollback article](https://getmoshi.app/articles/fix-mosh-scrollback)
- **tmux vs Herdr framing**: Moshi's own guide says tmux "keeps processes alive and tells you nothing about them," while Herdr "tracks which agent panes are blocked, working, or done"; Herdr offers "standard scrollback" that's "clickable by design," plus purpose-built APIs (wait-on-status, read-pane-output) versus tmux's send-keys scripting. [tmux-or-herdr guide](https://getmoshi.app/guides/tmux-or-herdr)
- **Terminal emulator / rendering tech**: **not disclosed** in any fetched docs page — UNVERIFIED which VT/ANSI rendering library Moshi uses.
- **Who makes it**: Publisher is "Moshi Tech Ltd." No page found stating a relationship to the herdr authors (herdrdev/herdr on GitHub); Moshi's own comparison guide treats Herdr as a third-party integration, not its own product — **appears to be an independent company**, UNVERIFIED beyond that (no explicit "we are/aren't affiliated" statement found).

## 4. herdr's remote/terminal-streaming APIs (github.com/herdrdev/herdr, herdr.dev)

- **CLI streaming commands** (confirmed via herdr.dev/docs/cli-reference): 
  - `herdr terminal session observe <target> [--cols N] [--rows N]` — read-only NDJSON stream of `terminal.frame` records (base64-encoded ANSI bytes), ending in `terminal.closed`; multiple observers allowed concurrently.
  - `herdr terminal session control <target> [--takeover] [--cols N] [--rows N]` — writable stream; accepts NDJSON commands `terminal.input`, `terminal.resize`, `terminal.scroll`, `terminal.release`; single controller unless `--takeover`.
  [CLI reference](https://herdr.dev/docs/cli-reference/)
- **Socket API** (herdr.dev/docs/socket-api): NDJSON over local Unix sockets, default `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock` (named sessions under `~/.config/herdr/sessions/<name>/herdr.sock`). `PaneInfo` carries scroll metrics: `{"offset_from_bottom": 12, "max_offset_from_bottom": 240, "viewport_rows": 30}`, with `offset_from_bottom == 0` meaning at-bottom. Event subscription `pane.scroll_changed` pushes these metrics on change (plus `pane.created/updated/closed/focused/moved/exited/agent_detected/output_matched/agent_status_changed`). [Socket API docs](https://herdr.dev/docs/socket-api/)
- **Remote/mobile**: docs mention `herdr --remote workbox` (SSH-based attach to a remote herdr instance using local keybindings) and a `--handoff` flag for live session transfer to an updated server — but no herdr-native mobile/WebSocket client was found; no `herdr-client.sock` or `persistence-remote` terminology was found in fetched docs (UNVERIFIED / may not exist as named). No `pane.scroll` command name was found distinct from `terminal.scroll`; treat `pane.scroll` as UNVERIFIED naming vs. confirmed `terminal.scroll`.

## 5. Prior art: server-side state + diff sync over a plain socket

- **tmux control mode (`tmux -CC`)**: server-authoritative pane state pushed over a control protocol to a client (used by iTerm2); relevant precedent for "diff-sync over a normal reliable socket," but requires a reliable stream (works over SSH/WS, not suited to lossy mobile links the way mosh is). [HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25740217)
- **Eternal Terminal (ET)**: TCP-based persistent-session tool; includes a "headless terminal multiplexer" (HTM) that tracks tab/pane state so a client reattaching gets restored state — closer analog to what merry wants (state resync over TCP/WS) but ET itself doesn't do frame-diffing the way mosh does. [eternalterminal.dev](https://eternalterminal.dev/)
- **xterm.js `addon-serialize`**: serializes an xterm.js buffer (screen + alt-screen + cursor) to a string/HTML blob for restore; directly relevant as a pattern for "reconstruct full terminal state from a snapshot," though it's a JS/web library, marked experimental. [addon-serialize](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/tree/master/addons/addon-serialize)
- **ttyd, wezterm mux, ghostty**: no strong documentary evidence surfaced in this pass connecting them to a diff-sync architecture comparable to mosh/SSP — UNVERIFIED, would need dedicated follow-up if wanted.

- **SwiftTerm** (migueldeicaza/SwiftTerm): MIT-licensed, mature (~7 years, 1300+ commits, 32 releases), includes a UI-agnostic VT100/xterm engine plus iOS (UIKit) and macOS (AppKit) front-ends usable from SwiftUI via wrapping. Used by commercial SSH apps: Secure Shellfish, La Terminal, CodeEdit. Scrollback support specifics not documented in the fetched README excerpt — UNVERIFIED exact buffer limits, but the engine is a full terminal emulator so in-memory scrollback is expected to be supported at some configurable depth. [SwiftTerm README](https://github.com/migueldeicaza/SwiftTerm/blob/main/README.md), [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com/migueldeicaza/SwiftTerm)
- No other actively-maintained Swift-native VT100 emulator libraries were surfaced in this pass; alternatives would mean wrapping a C library (e.g., libvterm) yourself — UNVERIFIED whether that's better than SwiftTerm for this use case.

<result># Merry codebase map — pane/session rendering pipeline

## 1. Pane/session content: phone → bridge → backend

- **Poll loop**: `ios/cmux/Layout/WorkspaceLayoutView.swift:958-982` — `Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 3.0, repeats: true)`. Every 3s: the focused surface is read every cycle, background surfaces every 5th cycle (~15s); `surface.list` is also refreshed every 5th cycle. `fetchContent` (`:985-1002`) dispatches to `appState.readSurfaceText` (or `readBrowserURL` for browser surfaces) and, for the focused Claude surface, also `loadClaudeTranscript`.
- **Depths**: focused = `AppState.focusedHistoryLines = 1500` (`AppState.swift:660`), background = `50` (`WorkspaceLayoutView.swift:992-993`). On explicit `focusSurface(_:)` (`AppState.swift:491-510`) a deep read is fired immediately rather than waiting for the timer. Sending input schedules a 1.5s "activity probe" read (`AppState.swift:576-591`) so the working indicator reacts quickly.
- **RPC call**: `AppState.readSurfaceText` (`AppState.swift:613-655`) sends `surface.read_text {surface_id, lines, workspace_id}`. A monotonically increasing `readSeq` per surface guards against out-of-order responses overwriting newer content (`:614-615, 631`). Trim/cap runs off-main (`Task.detached`) then applied on `MainActor`.
- **Diff/working-heuristic**: `previous != content` decides whether to publish `surfaceContent[surfaceID]` (`:648-649`, avoids no-op `@Published` fires) and, only when `agentStatus[surfaceID] == nil` and the read depth is unchanged, whether to flip `workingSurfaces` (`:637-644`) — i.e. cmux surfaces get a "diff = working" heuristic, herdr surfaces (which carry `agent_status`) don't.
- **Trim/cap**: `trimTerminalText` strips trailing per-line whitespace and trailing blank lines (`:807-818`); `capHistoryLines` caps to `maxHistoryLines = 5000` (`:822-828`) "so a UITextView can't lay out" arbitrarily long text.
- **Bridge dispatch**: `bridge/internal/ws/handler.go:120-150` runs one goroutine reading `wsjson` commands and a select loop writing backend events + command responses. `dispatch` (`:154-160`) calls `be.Handle(method, params)`.
- **cmux backend**: `bridge/internal/backend/cmux/cmux.go:167-181` proxies every method verbatim to cmux's own Unix socket except `claude.transcript`/`agent.transcript`, which is bridge-local (`:169-171, 183-222`). Per `shared/protocol.md:211-217`, cmux's own `surface.read_text` returns the last N rows **including terminal scrollback**, but "full-screen TUIs like claude-code repaint a fixed viewport and keep little/no terminal scrollback, so for those it returns roughly the visible screen" — a cmux limitation noted in `AppState.swift:605-612` too. Uncertain: exactly how cmux computes/wraps that text (columns, ANSI) is outside this repo (cmux app itself).
- **herdr backend**: `bridge/internal/backend/herdr/translate.go:328-359` (`readText`) calls `pane.read {source:"recent", lines, strip_ansi:true}`. `clampReadLines` (`:361-370`) bounds `lines` to the pane's `Scroll.ViewportRows` **only when the pane is running a recognized agent** — because "a deeper read on an idle alternate-screen agent makes herdr scroll the user's live pane to page its history" (comment `:323-327`). Plain shells are not clamped, so herdr shells can still return real scrollback; agent panes (Claude, opencode, etc. under herdr) cannot — history for those must come from `claude.transcript`.
- **Publishing**: `@Published var surfaceContent: [String:String]` (`AppState.swift:22`) and `@Published var workingSurfaces` (`:27`) are the two properties the polling loop feeds; `claudeTranscript`/`claudeCardText` (`:82,87`) are the transcript-derived ones (section 3).

## 2. Rendering on the phone

- **Not a terminal emulator.** `ios/cmux/Layout/TerminalTextView.swift` is a `UIViewRepresentable` wrapping a plain `UITextView` (`:15-74`), chosen over SwiftUI `Text`/`AttributedString` specifically for text selection and tappable links (`:4-7`). There is no ANSI/SGR color parsing anywhere in the iOS code — herdr strips ANSI server-side (`strip_ansi: true`, translate.go:349); cmux's own stripping is opaque to this repo. All text renders as flat white/opacity-scaled monospace (`TerminalTextRenderer.build`, `:339-349`): `UIFont.monospacedSystemFont(ofSize:weight:.regular)`, fixed size (`fontSize` param, scaled by `contentScale` in `PaneCardView.swift:142` — 9pt focused/7pt unfocused × scale). No Dynamic Type support (`fontSize` is a fixed CGFloat, not `.font(.body)`); no color at all, so exit-code coloring, diffs, syntax highlighting, etc. are all invisible.
- **No column/row negotiation.** There is no `cols`/`rows`/resize RPC anywhere in `shared/protocol.md`, `AppState.swift`, or the bridge; the phone never tells the Mac its width. Text wrapping is whatever the backend PTY/terminal already produced (fixed-width rows from cmux/herdr), then UITextView further soft-wraps that at whatever width the card happens to have on screen — i.e. double-wrapping with no coordination. `TerminalTextRenderer.joinedAcrossWraps` (`:451-494`) is a heuristic hack that re-joins URLs that got hard-wrapped by the *upstream* PTY width, inferred from "longest row in this snapshot" (`:461-465`) — evidence the width mismatch is a known, worked-around problem, not solved.
- **Follow-bottom / scroll**: `ScrollFollow.swift` — `autoScroll` toggles off only on a real (non-programmatic) scroll away from bottom (`follow`, `:43-45`); `bottomThreshold = 24pt` (`:14`). `TerminalTextView.Coordinator.apply` (`TerminalTextView.swift:163-219`) is where every new snapshot lands: it rebuilds the whole `NSAttributedString` off-main (`render`, `:147-161`) then does a **full replace** `tv.attributedText = attr` (`:183`) on every poll — not incremental/appended. Three scroll behaviors after that assignment:
  1. If a text selection is active, skip applying entirely and retry later (`:167-171`).
  2. If a search is active, jump to the current match, ignoring bottom-follow (`:191-203`).
  3. Else: if `autoScroll`, `scrollToBottom` (`:205-206`, double-deferred to next runloop, `:221-234`); else if the new text is a strict superset ending in the old text (`isPrepend`, `:178-179` — i.e. history was prepended), shift offset by exactly the added height to keep the same lines on screen (`:207-218`); otherwise the raw scroll offset is left as-is against completely different content (see gap #2 below).
- **Places that reset/jump scroll**: `pinToBottom` on every auto-follow poll (`:236-249`); `handleScrollRequest` explicit jump-to-bottom button (`PaneCardView.swift:176-192`, wired via `scrollToBottomRequest`); opening `TranscriptSheetView` always calls `loadClaudeTranscript(showsSpinner:true)` on `.onAppear` (`PaneCardView.swift:316-321`); `resetSessionState()` wipes `surfaceContent`/`claudeTranscript`/etc. entirely on bridge disconnect/switch (`AppState.swift:416-452`).

## 3. Claude transcript path

- `AppState.loadClaudeTranscript` (`AppState.swift:673-764`) sends `claude.transcript {surface_id, max_messages:300, known_fingerprint}`. A 15s timeout safety-net clears in-flight/loading flags if the bridge never answers (`:688-697`). `claudeTranscriptSeq`/`claudeTranscriptAppliedSeq` guard against out-of-order application, mirroring the `readSeq` pattern.
- **Full-file-with-fingerprint-cache model, not a tail/push.** Bridge side (`bridge/internal/claude/transcript.go`): `Resolver.Render` (`:135-208`) resolves the surface → session → `.jsonl` path (5-strategy fallback documented in `:210-235`, backed by cmux's hook store `~/.cmuxterm/claude-hook-sessions.json`, `hookstore.go:13-48`), computes a `fingerprint` from path+mtime+size+maxMessages (`:344-348`), and if it equals the client's `known_fingerprint` returns `{unchanged:true}` with no text — "cheap to poll every cycle." Otherwise it reads the **tail** of the file (`readTail`, bounded to `maxTranscriptFileBytes = 32MB`, `:26,354-369`), renders only the last `max_messages` (default 200, client-capped 2000, `cmux.go:225-234`) turns via `renderJSONL` (`:447-502`), and caps the rendered text to `maxRenderBytes = 128KB` tail (`:429-442`) — "so a long session can't produce a payload that blows past WebSocket message-size limits." A small 8-entry render cache (`:35-71`) avoids re-rendering on repeated identical reads.
- iOS composes the card as transcript + a `liveScreenDivider` + the live terminal mirror (`recomposeClaudeCard`, `AppState.swift:774-787`), and `cardText(for:)` (`:797-802`) switches per-surface between `claudeCardText` (Claude) and `surfaceContent` (everything else) based on `surface.isClaudeAgent` **currently**, not historically.
- **Dispatch**: no special-case remains in `ws/handler.go` — it's routed generically through `be.Handle`; the special-case lives inside each backend (`cmux.go:168-171`, `herdr/translate.go:87-88`).
- **isClaudeAgent / resume_binding**: `Surface.agentKind` comes from `resume_binding.kind` (`AppState.swift:1455`), `isClaudeAgent = agentKind == "claude"` (`:1446`). `agentStatus` (`:1456`, herdr only) is separate and drives the working indicator when present.

## 4. opencode / other agents

- **Not present on this branch (`rename/merry`) or `main`.** `rg -i opencode` over the working tree returns nothing outside `.claude/worktrees/*`.
- It **does** exist on `worktree-opencode-sessions` (commit `7b1b8e3 feat: read opencode sessions like Claude Code sessions`, `git show worktree-opencode-sessions --stat`): new `bridge/internal/opencode/{opencode.go,processes.go}` + `bridge/internal/transcriptrender/render.go` (shared render code Claude was refactored onto), plus `bridge/internal/ws/transcript.go` (281 lines) and edits to the *old* `ws/handler.go`/`ws/server.go`.
- Approach (from the commit message and `opencode.go:1-100`): detects opencode via the tty↔process table (`processes.go`), not by title/text; resolves *which* session via the surface's title (`"OC | <title>"`) matched against opencode's SQLite DB (`~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`), queried by shelling out to the `sqlite3` CLI (explicitly avoiding cgo/pure-Go SQLite). Untitled sessions report `opencode_unidentified` and render empty rather than guessing.
- **Important gap**: this branch was cut from `28d86f1` (before `07bb0d4 feat: herdr backend, composite cmux+herdr bridge...`). It predates the current `backend.Backend` interface / `multi` package entirely and edits the old monolithic `ws/handler.go`/`ws/server.go` directly. It has **not** been rebased onto the herdr/multi backend architecture — merging it today means re-deriving it as a third backend-agnostic transcript source (like `claude.Resolver`) rather than a simple merge.

## 5. Push channel / message limits

- Only four push types exist (`bridge/internal/backend/backend.go:110` `Hub.Broadcast`, fanned out in `ws/handler.go:125-131`): `notification.created`, `backend.connected`/`disconnected`/`changed`, and `surface.updated` (herdr's `agent_status`/title changes, `herdr/backend.go:422`). **There is no push for raw pane/terminal output changes at all** — `surface.read_text` is polling-only; no `events.stream` method exists anywhere in the repo.

Outgoing (bridge→phone) has no explicit Go-side limit; the iOS client raises `task.maximumMessageSize = 8 * 1024 * 1024` (`BridgeClient.swift:195`) specifically because "large payloads like claude session transcripts... can exceed the default 1 MiB." `protocol.md:292-295` separately notes a ~16MB WebSocket transport ceiling for pasted images.

## 6. Concrete layout/scroll UX gaps

- **Full-text replace every poll, not incremental.** `TerminalTextView.Coordinator.apply` reassigns `tv.attributedText` wholesale on every 3s cycle even when only the tail changed (`TerminalTextView.swift:183`); the `isPrepend` anchor logic (`:178-179, 207-218`) only recognizes the "old text is a suffix of new" case (history prepended while scrolled up). Any other kind of content substitution is not scroll-anchored.
- **Claude-mode toggle jumps the reader.** `cardText(for:)` (`AppState.swift:797-802`) switches the *entire* text source between `claudeCardText` and `surfaceContent` the instant `isClaudeAgent` flips (Claude Code exits/starts in a surface). This is neither an append nor a suffix relation, so a user scrolled up when that happens keeps their pixel offset applied to unrelated content — a silent scroll-position corruption, not caught by the `isPrepend` heuristic.

<result>## Report: Real Terminal View — herdr vs cmux

Both daemons running live on this Mac: **herdr** `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock` (v0.8.2, protocol 20, confirmed via `ping`), **cmux** app (pid 25602) + `cmux-bridge` (pid 72201) on `~/.local/state/cmux/cmux-501.sock` per `~/.config/cmux-bridge/config.json` (`socket_password:""`, `backend:"all"`). Bridge source: `bridge/internal/socket/client.go`, `bridge/internal/backend/{cmux,herdr}/`, `shared/protocol.md`.

### herdr

**1. Content read APIs.** `pane.read {pane_id, source, lines?, format?, strip_ansi?, raw?}`. `source` ∈ `visible|recent|recent_unwrapped|detection` (CLI shows dash, wire uses underscore for the middle one). Verified via `herdr pane read w1:p2 --source recent --lines 10 --format text|ansi`. Result shape (from `herdr api schema --json`, `PaneReadResult`): `{pane_id, workspace_id, tab_id, source, format, text, revision, truncated}` — no cursor field anywhere in the schema (only occurrence of the string "cursor" is the agent-kind enum value for Cursor CLI).

**2. ANSI/colors.** Yes — `--format ansi` returns real SGR/color escapes; verified output contained `\x1b[38;5;10m` etc. `--format text` strips them. Our bridge's herdr translation (`translate.go:349`) currently hardcodes `strip_ansi:true`, i.e. today it throws this away.

**3. Scrollback / live-pane disturbance.** `source:"recent"+lines:N` includes host scrollback for plain shell panes. **Confirmed gotcha** (already documented in `plans/herdr-backend.md` from an earlier session, and unchanged in v0.8.2): for an *idle* recognized agent pane, a deep `recent` read makes herdr physically scroll the pane to page history then back — visibly disturbs the user. Bridge already clamps `lines` to `scroll.viewport_rows` for agent panes; I did not repeat that live test (would disturb a pane) and relied on the prior verified finding + source.

**4. Scroll/cursor/size fields.** Live from `herdr pane list` / `herdr api snapshot`: `scroll:{offset_from_bottom, max_offset_from_bottom, viewport_rows}` per pane. No cols field on pane directly; cell dimensions come from `layouts[].panes[].rect:{x,y,width,height}` (cells). No cursor-position field anywhere in the schema.

**5. Push/stream of output.**
- `events.subscribe` global kinds include `pane_output_changed` in the `EventKind` enum, but it's **not actually subscribable** — I live-tested `events.subscribe {subscriptions:[{"kind":"pane_output_changed"}]}` and the server closed the connection (`BrokenPipeError`) right after. Subscribable kinds are only `pane.output_matched` (pattern-match via `wait-output`), `pane.agent_status_changed`, and **`pane.scroll_changed`** `{pane_id, workspace_id, scroll:{offset_from_bottom, max_offset_from_bottom, viewport_rows}}` (new finding — scroll-position push exists and is cheap, could drive a live scroll indicator).
- **Real frame streaming exists**: `herdr terminal session observe <pane_id> --cols N --rows N` (CLI subprocess over the separate `herdr-client.sock` wire protocol). Live-tested against `w1:p2`, captured NDJSON records shaped:
  ```json
  {"type":"terminal.frame","seq":1,"width":80,"height":24,"encoding":"ansi","full":true,"bytes":"<base64 PTY bytes>"}
  ```
  Decoded `bytes` is raw terminal output including cursor-position/clear escapes (`\x1b[2J\x1b[1;1H...`) — genuinely a renderable ANSI byte stream, not a structured grid. `herdr terminal session control <target> [--takeover] --cols --rows` is the write-side (input + resize); not exercised (would be invasive). This is the path to a real terminal view.

**6. Resize.** `pane.resize {direction, amount, pane_id}` only resizes a **split ratio**, not terminal cols/rows (confirmed via schema `PaneResizeParams`). True terminal-cell resize appears to live only in `terminal session control --cols/--rows` (untested, control-only). No standalone `pane.set_size`/cols-rows RPC found in the schema.

### cmux

**1. Content read APIs.** Only `surface.read_text {surface_id, lines?, scrollback?, workspace_id?}` (per `shared/protocol.md` and live testing) — no `surface.read_screen`, `surface.stream`, `surface.resize`, `surface.cursor`, `events.subscribe`, `system.methods`/`rpc.list`; all live-tested and returned `{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"method_not_found"}}`, confirming the socket has a fixed method table with none of these.

**2. ANSI/colors.** **No.** Live test on a plain shell surface (`790F0B91-…`, workspace "npm run start", no `resume_binding`) with `surface.read_text {lines:5, format:"ansi"}` returned identical plain text to the no-format call — `format` is silently ignored, no ESC bytes anywhere in `text` or `base64` (which is just base64 of the same plain text). Scrollback / live-pane disturbance.** `source:"recent"+lines:N` includes host scrollback for plain shell panes. **Confirmed gotcha** (already documented in `plans/herdr-backend.md` from an earlier session, and unchanged in v0.8.2): for an *idle* recognized agent pane, a deep `recent` read makes herdr physically scroll the pane to page history then back — visibly disturbs the user. # Socket/CLI Methods for Terminal Surfaces

Based on the documentation provided, the reference lists the following surface-related methods:

## Documented Methods

**Surface management:**
- `surface.split` (with `direction` parameter)
- `surface.list` (list all surfaces in current workspace)
- `surface.focus` (with `surface_id` parameter)
- `surface.send_text` (with `text` and optional `surface_id` parameters)
- `surface.send_key` (with `key` and optional `surface_id` parameters)

**Pane operations:**
- `pane.surfaces` (list surfaces in focused pane)

## Notable Omissions

The documentation does **not** include methods for:
- Reading screen text (`surface.read_text` or similar)
- Screenshots or screen capture
- Streaming or subscribing to output/events
- Event subscriptions
- Resize operations
- Cursor control
- Scroll commands

The reference mentions `"every command is available through both interfaces"` (CLI and socket), but the documented methods shown are limited to workspace, split, input, notification, sidebar metadata, and utility categories. No protocol version is explicitly stated in the provided content.

The project was renamed cmux → **merry** (2026-08-27, full identifier rename). Repo is `itsmaleen/merry`; iOS lives in `ios/merry/`, project `ios/merry.xcodeproj`, target/scheme `merry`, bundle id `dev.itsmaleen.merry`.

The `merry` scheme fails destination resolution from CLI ("Supported platforms for the buildables in the current scheme is empty" / "Found no destinations"). Build the target directly against the simulator SDK instead:

`cd ios && xcodebuild -project merry.xcodeproj -target merry -sdk iphonesimulator26.5 -configuration Debug build`

Products land in `ios/build/Debug-iphonesimulator/merry.app`. Bundle id: `dev.itsmaleen.merry`.

Runtime smoke test: `xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 17 Pro"` → `simctl install <app>` → `simctl launch "iPhone 17 Pro" dev.itsmaleen.merry` → verify alive via `simctl spawn "iPhone 17 Pro" launchctl list | grep dev.itsmaleen.merry`. The app's real UI needs a live bridge, so headless launch only reaches the pairing screen — enough to confirm no launch crash.

**The Xcode project is generated by XcodeGen** (`ios/project.yml`, `xcodegen` is installed at /opt/homebrew/bin). After adding/renaming source files or the app icon, `cd ios && xcodegen generate` regenerates `merry.xcodeproj` — far cleaner than hand-editing the pbxproj. xcodegen auto-wires `ios/merry/Assets.xcassets` (the AppIcon) as a resource. (Before the rename the pbxproj was hand-edited; now prefer regenerating.)

App icon: `ios/merry/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset` holds a single 1024 universal icon (the merry ram, from itsmaleen/merry's packages/ui/build/icon.png, flattened full-bleed so iOS rounds it). CFBundleDisplayName = "merry".

Watch disk space: booting a sim + install can exhaust the volume and then ALL Bash fails with ENOSPC (output files can't be written). #!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs the iOS logic tests. The app target has no XCTest bundle, so the pure,
# UIKit-free pieces are compiled and run directly with swiftc.
set -euo pipefail

  "$tmp/$name"
}
